opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. When I think about the ultimate form of a world model, I think of it as a simulator of the world that an AI can carry around in its head. Given the current state of the world and some action, whether that's a robot moving its arm, a car changing lanes, or a person opening a door, the model should predict what happens next, and do so accurately enough that you can make decisions based on it.

Today most of what we call world models are video-based. You give the model some frames and maybe a text prompt or an action, and it generates future frames that look plausible. That's a great start, because video is the richest data we have about how the physical world works. But I don't think pixels are the end goal. The ultimate world model has to capture physics correctly: objects have mass, things fall, liquids flow, collisions behave the way they should. It has to be consistent over long horizons, so if you walk around a room and come back, the room is still the same. And it has to respond to actions faithfully, because the whole point is to let an agent ask "what if I do this?" and get a trustworthy answer.

So in its ultimate form, I'd say a world model is something like a universal, learned physics engine plus a renderer, trained from data rather than handcrafted. It should work across scales and domains, from a kitchen to a factory floor to a city street, and it should be multimodal, not just vision but also touch, sound, and language, because humans understand the world through all of those.

Why does this matter so much? I believe the next big wave of AI is physical AI: robots, autonomous vehicles, smart spaces. Those systems can't learn everything by trial and error in the real world. It's too slow, too expensive, and sometimes dangerous. A good world model lets them practice in imagination, generate rare and edge-case scenarios, and evaluate policies before deployment. In a way it plays the same role for physical AI that large-scale internet text played for language models.

We're still far from that ultimate form. Current models hallucinate physics, drift over time, and are expensive to run. But the trajectory is clear, and I think each year we're getting meaningfully closer to a model you could genuinely call a simulator of the world.

r001.rationale: The response says agents can practice in imagination and evaluate policies, but does not identify learning through the model whatever one wants to learn in the real world as a defining capability.

r002.rationale: It describes a world simulator with a renderer, but does not convey creating a Matrix-like simulated reality on demand.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the ultimate form of a world model is something like a simulator of the physical world that you can query the way we query a language model today, but instead of predicting the next word, it predicts the next state of the world.

Let me unpack that a little. A world model, at its core, takes in a description of a situation, whether that's a video, sensor readings, a text prompt, or an action a robot is about to take, and it predicts what happens next. Right now the models we build do this reasonably well for short horizons and for scenes that look like the training data. But the ultimate version would understand the underlying physics and causality well enough that you could ask it about situations it has never seen. You could say, "Here is a factory floor, here is a new robot design, what happens if it picks up this object from this angle?" and get an answer you can trust, with uncertainty when it is genuinely uncertain.

There are a few properties I think that final form needs to have. First, it has to be controllable. It is not enough to generate plausible video. You need to be able to specify actions, camera positions, object properties, and have the model respect them precisely. Second, it has to be consistent over long horizons. Objects should not disappear, mass should not change, a cup you put down should still be there ten minutes later. Third, it needs to be multimodal, because the world is not just pixels. It is forces, sounds, temperatures, language. And fourth, and this is the one I think about most, it has to be useful for decision making. The whole point is that an embodied agent can imagine many possible futures, evaluate them, and pick the best action before it acts in the real world, where mistakes are expensive or dangerous.

If you get all of that, then the world model becomes the foundation for physical AI in the same way that large language models became the foundation for digital AI. You train robots in it, you test autonomous vehicles in it, you generate the data for rare events you could never collect safely in reality. In that sense I do not think of the ultimate world model as a model that replaces the real world. I think of it as a model that lets machines learn from the real world much faster and much more safely than they could otherwise.

We are still early. Today the gap between what the model generates and what is actually physically correct is still significant. But the trajectory feels similar to where language models were a few years ago, and I think that is why so many of us are excited about it.

r001.rationale: It describes training robots in the world model and says it lets machines learn from the real world faster and more safely, communicating learning through the model as a defining capability.

r002.rationale: It describes a queryable physical-world simulator, but does not communicate creating a Matrix-like simulated reality on demand.

astra-6.text:
I think the ultimate form of a world model is a simulator that lets an intelligent agent understand how the world changes in response to its actions. It’s not just about generating a video that looks realistic. If I move an object, push something, or take a different path, the model should predict the consequences consistently.

And because the world is uncertain, it shouldn’t predict only one future. It should represent different possible outcomes. An agent could then use that model to imagine alternatives, plan, and learn before acting in the real world.

So, to me, the ultimate goal is a model that combines perception, prediction, and action—a model useful enough that an agent can rely on it to make decisions.

r001.rationale: It says an agent can learn before acting, but does not identify learning through the model whatever it wants to learn in the real world as a defining capability.

r002.rationale: It describes a simulator for predicting outcomes, but does not envision creating a Matrix-like simulated reality on demand.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the ultimate form of a world model is a simulator that can predict how the world will evolve in response to actions. You give it an observation and a possible action, and it can imagine what happens next—not just one likely future, but a range of plausible futures.

The important thing is that it understands interactions. If I move an object, how does that affect the rest of the scene? If a robot takes a particular action, what changes, and what stays the same? A model like that would let an intelligent agent try things in imagination before acting in the real world.

It doesn’t necessarily need to reproduce every detail of reality. It needs to capture the things that matter for making decisions. To me, that’s the ultimate goal: a model that turns experience into the ability to anticipate, plan, and act.

r001.rationale: The response says an agent can try actions in imagination before acting, but does not identify learning what it wants to learn in the real world as a defining capability.

r002.rationale: It describes simulating possible futures, but does not envision creating a Matrix-like simulated reality on demand.
